text: The young republic had a rough start.
India lost a border war with China in 1962 and fought Pakistan in 1965.
In the mid-sixties, India was so short of food that it depended on grain shipments from America.
Then came the Green Revolution.
New high-yield wheat and rice, irrigation and fertilizer.
Within a decade, India was growing enough to feed itself.
Holding a bag of rice? From begging for grain to feeding a billion? Not bad.
In 1971, India backed the independence struggle in East Pakistan and won a short war.
A new country was born. Bangladesh.
In 1975, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi declared an emergency.
Elections were suspended, opposition leaders jailed, newspapers censored.
But when she finally called elections in 1977, the voters threw her out.
The voters remembered the picture symbols.
She came back to power in 1980.
In 1984, she was assassinated, and terrible violence against Sikhs followed in Delhi and
other cities.
For most of these years, India's economy was tightly controlled.
You needed government permission to make almost anything.
People called it the License Raj.
In 1991, India almost ran out of money.
Its foreign reserves could pay for only about three weeks of imports.
To get an emergency loan, the government flew 47 tons of gold to the Bank of England.
Cargo. 47 tons of gold. Destination. London.
Keep it quiet. Wait, didn't the British take enough already?
This time, we're getting it back.
